narrative.text: Acknowledges the WHO Global TB Programme staff who wrote each chapter of the child and adolescent TB handbook, the many external contributors and reviewers, and funding from Unitaid, USAID and the US CDC.
A list of abbreviations used in the child and adolescent TB handbook, mostly TB and HIV medicines, tests and programme terms.

Defines key terms used in the child and adolescent TB operational handbook, such as active case-finding, adherence, advanced HIV disease and adverse events. It goes on through diagnostic, treatment, disease severity and programme terms, ending with definitions of treatment outcomes, the tuberculin skin test and TB disease. Footnotes cite WHO reporting frameworks and outcome definitions.
A heading for chapter 1, the introduction.

Notes that children and young adolescents under 15 make up about 11% of TB cases, or 1.1 million a year, but fewer than half are notified, with the largest gap in children under 5 owing to diagnostic difficulties. It introduces the 2022 consolidated guidelines and defines a child as under 10 and an adolescent as 10–19 years.

Explains that TB in children is most common at ages 1–4, usually follows recent infection and signals ongoing community transmission, that infants face high risk of severe disease, and that adolescents often have adult-type disease and particular psychosocial needs.

States that the handbook aims to give practical guidance on implementing WHO recommendations on child and adolescent TB and to inform national policies and capacity building. It cites the UN high-level meeting targets for treating children with TB and providing preventive treatment.

Reports a survey of 182 end-users on barriers to implementing child TB recommendations and preferences for the handbook, who favoured practical content, translations, electronic versions and dissemination through webinars, regional consultations and online training.

Explains that the handbook follows the pathway from TB exposure to infection, disease, diagnosis and treatment, illustrated in a figure, and describes the chapters and colour-coded boxes for recommendations, key points and examples.
Identifies the handbook's audience as national TB programmes, child health, HIV and primary care programmes, paediatricians and other health workers, schools, civil society and educators.
A fragment of the chapter 2 heading on TB screening and contact investigation.

Introduces chapter 2, noting that about a quarter of the world's population is infected with TB and that 7.5 million children under 15 are newly infected each year. It defines contact investigation and argues that the case detection gap justifies systematic screening of risk groups.

Describes contact investigation for children and adolescents, stressing that household and close contacts of people with pulmonary TB should be systematically screened and citing the high risk of disease in infected young children without preventive treatment. It covers prioritising household contacts and planning and budgeting for facility- and community-based approaches. Country examples and boxes describe implementation experiences, including challenges such as reaching remote households and stigma. It ends with prerequisites for a community-based model from the CONTACT study in Uganda and Cameroon.

Explains the purpose of TB screening in children and adolescents and when it should be done, such as at every visit for those living with HIV and during contact investigation for household contacts. It describes screening tools, including symptom screening, chest X-ray and rapid molecular tests, and their use by age group. It covers practical considerations for screening child close contacts, including caregiver preferences. It ends by explaining when chest X-ray is needed before starting preventive treatment.

Describes TB screening of children living with HIV, who are at much higher risk of progression and death, using a symptom and contact screen at every visit with an algorithm and noted sensitivity and specificity. It covers other screening tests, implementation and screening of adolescents, and closes with key points on screening.
Introduces chapter 3 on preventing TB in children and adolescents through BCG vaccination, preventive treatment and infection control, with a pathway figure.

Describes BCG vaccine, which gives up to 90% protection against severe TB forms such as meningitis and miliary TB when given at birth and modest protection against infection. It summarises the WHO position paper recommendations on neonatal vaccination in high-burden settings and special groups. It describes local, regional and disseminated adverse events, including BCG-related immune reconstitution syndrome in people with HIV, and their management.

Covers TB preventive treatment in children and adolescents, defining TB infection, its global burden and the 5–10% lifetime risk of progression, higher in young children and people with HIV. The headings show it addresses target groups for preventive treatment, ruling out TB disease, testing for infection, the available regimens and child-friendly formulations, and practical implementation. A table explains how to manage missed doses for different regimens such as 3HP and 1HP. It ends by referring other issues, such as babies born to women with TB and ART choice, to other sections and the Module 1 handbook.

Explains TB infection prevention and control in health facilities, noting that adolescents can transmit like adults and that poor practices expose children, and that COVID-19 mask use may reduce stigma. It outlines administrative, environmental and respiratory protection measures and closes with key points on prevention.

Introduces the diagnostic chapter, explaining that children with presumptive TB need careful clinical assessment and that bacteriological confirmation is hard in young children because of few bacilli and difficulty producing sputum.

Notes that the diagnostic chapter covers drug-susceptible, drug-resistant, pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB, with pulmonary TB in children usually involving chest lymph nodes, and shows a pathway figure.

Lists the groups of children and adolescents at highest risk of TB disease, such as close contacts, under-fives and those with HIV or severe malnutrition, from the WHO operational handbook on TB in children and adolescents. It sets out the components of diagnosis, including history, examination, HIV testing, bacteriological testing and chest X-ray, and advises against a trial of TB treatment as a diagnostic method.

Defines pulmonary TB in children, including intrathoracic lymph node and miliary disease, and describes typical persistent symptoms, cough patterns and the importance of a TB contact history. It covers clinical examination signs suggestive of pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB and considerations during contact investigation. The section goes on to cover diagnostic tests and treatment decision algorithms for children who cannot be confirmed bacteriologically. It ends with an example of scoring under Algorithm B and definitions of the symptoms used in the algorithms, such as cough, fever, weight loss and tachycardia.

Defines extrapulmonary TB in children and notes it is common in young children and those with HIV, calling for urgent evaluation or referral of very ill children. It reproduces WHO recommendations on using Xpert MTB/RIF and Ultra on non-respiratory specimens such as CSF, lymph node aspirates and blood. A table lists typical presentations and investigations for different extrapulmonary sites, such as TB meningitis, miliary and abdominal TB.

Explains how TB disease severity is assessed in children, since those aged 3 months to 16 years with non-severe drug-susceptible TB can receive a shorter 4-month regimen. It defines non-severe disease by clinical and chest X-ray findings and stresses that assessing severity should not delay treatment.

Describes how to diagnose drug-resistant TB in children, emphasizing collection of respiratory or stool samples for rapid molecular tests that detect rifampicin resistance and the role of source-case information. It reproduces WHO recommendations on molecular tests for resistance to isoniazid, fluoroquinolones and other drugs. Key messages stress prioritizing bacteriological testing for all children with presumed TB.
A chapter title fragment on treating both drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB, pulmonary and extrapulmonary, in young people.

Introduces the treatment chapter, which covers regimens for drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB, TB meningitis and post-TB health, including the new 4-month regimen. It notes that treatment outcomes in children are generally excellent and that most child TB deaths occur in those never treated, with a figure illustrating the cascade from exposure to treatment.

Sets out the principles of managing drug-susceptible TB in children and adolescents, from medicine management and comorbidities to family involvement, adherence support and recording. It describes the recommended regimens, including the 4-month regimen for non-severe TB based on the SHINE trial, the rifapentine–moxifloxacin regimen for adolescents aged 12 and over, and a 6-month intensive regimen for TB meningitis. It also covers child-friendly fixed-dose formulations, dose adjustment as children gain weight, adverse events and monitoring. Key messages summarize these points and require all children treated for TB to be registered and reported to the national TB programme.

Describes the practical treatment of children with multidrug- and rifampicin-resistant TB, starting with estimates that tens of thousands of children develop MDR-TB each year yet few are diagnosed. It presents the WHO drug groupings and recommendations favouring the shorter all-oral bedaquiline regimen or individualized longer regimens, now with bedaquiline and delamanid allowed at all ages. It covers monitoring, adverse events and implementation issues. Key messages call for specimen collection, empirical treatment based on the source case, child-friendly formulations, avoiding injectables and social support for families.

Introduces post-TB health in children and adolescents, noting that consequences of TB can persist after treatment and need to be measured and managed. It describes long-term complications of TB meningitis, such as neurodisability, blindness and hormonal problems, with an end-of-treatment assessment table. It also covers assessment of post-TB lung disease using imaging and spirometry and tools for measuring health-related quality of life in children.
A section heading fragment on models of TB care for children and adolescents.

Explains that TB care for children in high-burden countries is often centralized and poorly integrated with child health, nutrition and HIV services, leading to missed cases and delays. It cites the 2018 Roadmap's key action on community engagement. It then reproduces WHO recommendations on decentralized, family-centred and integrated care and on community-based, lay-provider and video-supported treatment support.

Explains what decentralizing child and adolescent TB services means and the interventions needed, such as training health workers, access to diagnostics and medicines, and follow-up. It describes a flexible approach for national programmes, health workforce tasks at each level of care in a table, and integration with other child health services. The section includes country examples, such as integrating childhood TB into IMNCI services in Addis Ababa with a sharp rise in contact screening and preventive treatment. It notes that services including gastric aspiration can be decentralized to primary care with supporting packages.

Explains that many children with TB first seek care from private providers and that national programmes must engage the private sector. It sets out key actions from the WHO public–private mix roadmap applied to child TB, such as mapping providers, setting targets, funding and working with paediatric associations. A case study from India describes linking over 1100 children treated by private providers to free public fixed-dose combinations, with the proportion rising from 29% to 65%. It also notes challenges such as treatment delays, pharmacy hours and pill burden.

Introduces differentiated service delivery, a people-centred approach developed for HIV care, and how it can be applied to TB services for children and adolescents. It discusses aligning TB treatment and preventive therapy with multimonth antiretroviral dispensing and family-centred care, while noting risks of fewer screening opportunities. Illustrated examples show models for children receiving TB preventive treatment, such as a child contact of a caregiver with HIV and TB supported by SMS.

Describes how health emergencies such as COVID-19 disrupted TB services, citing the fall in notified TB cases from 7.1 million in 2019 to 5.8 million in 2020. It discusses the direct and indirect effects of emergencies on child and adolescent TB services and outlines measures to maintain care. It concludes that mitigation approaches should take account of the particular needs of children and adolescents with or exposed to TB.
Introduces the chapter on special situations in managing TB in children and adolescents.

Lists the special situations covered in the chapter and opens section 7.1 on TB in children and adolescents living with HIV, who face higher risks of TB infection, disease and death. It covers HIV testing recommendations, TB screening with symptom screening and chest radiography, and prevention through preventive treatment for household contacts. Later parts address treatment and co-management with antiretroviral therapy. It ends with guidance on recognising and managing TB immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, including when to continue treatment, use anti-inflammatory drugs or refer.

Describes the contribution of TB to maternal mortality and adverse pregnancy and perinatal outcomes, and covers TB screening for pregnant women living with HIV with a table of screening tool accuracy. It then addresses diagnosis and management of congenital and neonatal TB. It closes with care for well newborns of mothers with TB, including preventive treatment, referral for MDR/RR-TB exposure and infection control.

Covers palliative care for children and adolescents with TB, starting from the 2014 World Health Assembly resolution calling for better access to palliative care. It describes circumstances in which children with TB may need palliative care and actions to make it available. A table gives examples of managing symptoms such as breathlessness and cough in children with advanced lung disease.

Describes the needs of adolescents with TB, who often have infectious adult-type disease and face stigma, peer pressure, comorbidities and risk behaviours. Sections follow a framework of physical and mental health, connectedness, safety and support, education and skills, agency and resilience, and substance use with late presentation to care. Each area sets out actions for adolescent-friendly services. The block ends by calling for collaboration with other sectors on basic needs such as food security and continued schooling.

Discusses TB as a cause or comorbidity of severe pneumonia in young children, citing a systematic review finding TB in about 5-10% of under-fives with pneumonia in endemic countries. It notes that clinical features have low specificity, and includes boxes on implications for implementation and findings of the TB-Speed Pneumonia study on Xpert Ultra testing.

Explains the two-way link between undernutrition and TB in children, citing estimates that about 19% of TB cases are attributable to undernourishment and varied TB prevalence among acutely malnourished children. It covers diagnosis and treatment of TB in malnourished children and nutritional care for children and adolescents with TB. Key points include evaluating children with severe acute malnutrition who fail to gain weight for TB and using a 6-month regimen for them.

The reference list for the operational handbook on managing TB in children and adolescents, with 230 citations including WHO TB reports and guidelines and studies on paediatric TB, HIV, pregnancy and malnutrition.
An annex listing selected resources on child and adolescent TB, including the WHO roadmap, operational handbooks, training materials and research and implementation projects such as TB-Speed.

An annex explaining how to give, read and interpret a tuberculin skin test by the Mantoux method using 5 tuberculin units. It covers the injection technique, measuring induration and thresholds for a positive result. It also discusses causes of false-positive and false-negative results.

An annex describing respiratory and non-respiratory specimens for diagnosing TB in children and adolescents, with tables giving each procedure, suitable age group, minimum volume and best collection time.

An annex giving standard operating procedures for collecting samples from children for rapid molecular TB testing by expectoration, gastric aspiration, nasopharyngeal aspiration and sputum induction. It opens with biosafety and infection-control precautions for these aerosol-generating procedures, such as dedicated ventilated rooms, respirators and disinfection. Each method then has a background note and step-by-step instructions for preparing the child, carrying out the procedure and handling the specimen. The annex closes with advice on obtaining specimens from young children who cannot expectorate and on sterilizing reusable equipment.

An annex presenting treatment decision algorithms for children under 10 with suspected pulmonary TB, starting with how the scoring models were built from pooled individual patient data and set at 85% sensitivity. It explains the triage steps for danger signs, high-risk children and rapid molecular testing that come before scoring. Two algorithms are shown, one for settings with chest X-ray and one without, assigning points to symptoms and radiographic features with a threshold of more than 10 for starting treatment. Operational guidance follows, including age-specific definitions of signs such as fast breathing and a worked scoring example.

An annex tabulating weight-band dosing of second-line medicines for multidrug-resistant TB in children and adolescents under 46 kg, grouped as in WHO regimens. Introductory notes cover preferring child-friendly dispersible tablets, dissolving tablets in water to give measured volumes, and seeking expert advice for infants. The table gives daily doses, formulations and usual maximum doses for drugs such as levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, bedaquiline and linezolid. Footnotes explain special cases, including pyridoxine use and giving carbapenems only with clavulanate.

An annex table listing tools and timing for neurodevelopmental, neurocognitive, functional and behavioural testing of children at the end of TB meningitis treatment. It notes that these tools are not adapted for low- and middle-income countries and closes with sources and WHO contact details.

The front matter of the WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis, Module 5: management of TB in children and adolescents (2022), with the ISBN and licence page, citation, disclaimers and a table of contents covering screening, prevention, diagnosis, treatment, models of care, special situations and annexes.
